primary_citation.popular_name: Failure to Obey a Peace Officer's Lawful Order

structural_location.section_history: Most recent amendment: Stats. 2022, Ch. 295, Sec. 3 (AB 2956) Effective January 1, 2023

(a)_lawful_order_of_uniformed_peace_offi.verbatim: It is unlawful to willfully fail or refuse to comply with a lawful order, signal, or direction of a peace officer, as defined in Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 830) of Title 3 of Part 2 of the Penal Code, when that peace officer is in uniform and is performing duties pursuant to any of the provisions of this code, or to refuse to submit to a lawful inspection pursuant to this code.
elements_of_offense: ELEMENT 1 — WILLFULLY: The failure or refusal must be willful. Inadvertent or accidental non-compliance does not satisfy this element.
ELEMENT 2 — FAIL OR REFUSE TO COMPLY: There must be actual non-compliance with the order or signal or direction. (Or, in the inspection variant, refusal to submit to a lawful inspection.)

ELEMENT 3 — LAWFUL ORDER, SIGNAL, OR DIRECTION: The order, signal, or direction must itself be lawful. An UNLAWFUL order is not within the scope of § 2800(a). The lawfulness of the order is the threshold legal question and is the most-litigated element.

ELEMENT 4 — PEACE OFFICER AS DEFINED IN PENAL CODE § 830 et seq.: The person giving the order must qualify as a 'peace officer' under Penal Code § 830 et seq. Not every uniformed person is a peace officer; the Penal Code's definition is statutory and enumerated.

ELEMENT 5 — IN UNIFORM: The peace officer must be IN UNIFORM at the time of giving the order. A plainclothes officer's order does not trigger § 2800(a) — though other Vehicle Code or Penal Code provisions may apply.

ELEMENT 6 — PERFORMING DUTIES PURSUANT TO ANY OF THE PROVISIONS OF THIS CODE: The peace officer must be performing Vehicle Code duties at the time of giving the order. An order pursuant to some other code (Penal Code, Health & Safety Code, etc.) does not trigger § 2800(a).
(a)_lawful_order_of_uniformed_peace_offi.doctrinal_significance: All six elements must be satisfied for § 2800(a) to apply. Failure on ANY element means § 2800(a) does not apply. The Vehicle Code duties requirement is structurally important: not every interaction with a uniformed peace officer falls under § 2800(a) — only those connected to Vehicle Code enforcement.

(b)_out_of_service_orders.verbatim_summary: Subsection (b) makes it unlawful to fail or refuse to comply with a lawful out-of-service order issued by an authorized CHP employee or other authorized enforcement officer. Special provisions apply to drivers of hazardous materials vehicles requiring placards under § 27903 and to drivers of passenger vehicles designed to transport 16+ passengers including the driver.
(b)_out_of_service_orders.applies_to: Commercial vehicle operations, particularly hazardous materials and passenger transport

(c)_federal_dot_out_of_service_orders.verbatim: It is unlawful to fail or refuse to comply with a lawful out-of-service order issued by the United States Secretary of the Department of Transportation.

(d)_out_of_service_order_definition.verbatim: 'Out-of-Service order' means a declaration by an authorized enforcement officer of a federal, state, Canadian, Mexican, or local jurisdiction that a driver, a commercial motor vehicle, or a motor carrier operation is out-of-service pursuant to Section 386.72, 392.5, 392.9a, 395.13, or 396.9 of Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations, state law, or the North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria.

(e)_commercial_vehicle_inspection_compli.verbatim: It is unlawful for a driver of a commercial vehicle subject to inspection under this code to fail to comply with any vehicle inspection testing and associated procedures as required by an authorized member of the California Highway Patrol.

The audit asks: was § 2800(a) actually applicable to the events of that day? Were all six elements of the (a) offense satisfied? factor_audits.what_the_statute_requires: The failure or refusal to comply must be WILLFUL — done knowingly and intentionally, not by accident, mistake, or confusion.
factor_audits.audit_question: On June 16, 2023, was the steward's response to the officers' presence willful non-compliance with a specific order, OR was it a response to confusion, surprise, or the absence of a clearly stated order?
factor_audits.audit_status: FLAGGED — requires steward review of the actual sequence of events to determine whether 'willful non-compliance' is the right characterization.

factor_audits.what_the_statute_requires: There must be a specific order, signal, or direction that the steward actually failed or refused to comply with.
factor_audits.audit_question: On June 16, 2023, what specific orders, signals, or directions were given by the officers, and which one(s) is the alleged § 2800 violation based on?
factor_audits.audit_status: FLAGGED — the specificity of the alleged order matters. Vague or implicit 'orders' are harder to prosecute under § 2800.

factor_audits.factor_id: ELEMENT 3 — Lawfulness of the order (THE THRESHOLD ELEMENT)
factor_audits.what_the_statute_requires: The order, signal, or direction must itself be LAWFUL. An order that exceeds the officer's lawful authority is not within § 2800(a). Lawfulness is judged against the officer's statutory authority, the Fourth Amendment / Cal. Const. Art. I § 13 (search and seizure), and the lawful scope of any underlying detention.
factor_audits.what_the_record_shows: Per project_june16_2023_timeline.md and project_familylaw_orchestration.md, the June 16, 2023 incident involved a coordinated setup with Christina pre-positioned, mother directing APD, a car purchase pretext, an ice cream pretext, and a 20-minute officer arrival. The question of whether the officers had any lawful basis for the contact at all — and therefore whether any orders given during the contact were 'lawful' under § 2800 — is the threshold question.
factor_audits.audit_question: Was there any lawful basis for the officers' presence and contact with the steward on June 16, 2023? If the contact was not supported by a lawful basis (no probable cause, no reasonable suspicion, no warrant, no consent), then any orders given during the contact were NOT lawful within the meaning of § 2800(a), and § 2800(a) cannot have been violated.
factor_audits.audit_status: CRITICAL — load-bearing audit item. The lawfulness-of-the-order element is the threshold legal question for any § 2800(a) charge. If the underlying contact was not lawful, the orders given during the contact were not lawful, and § 2800(a) does not apply regardless of the steward's response.

factor_audits.factor_id: ELEMENT 4 — Peace officer status under Penal Code § 830 et seq.
factor_audits.what_the_statute_requires: The person giving the order must be a 'peace officer' as defined in Penal Code Chapter 4.5 (commencing with § 830). The Penal Code enumerates specific categories of peace officers; not every uniformed person qualifies.
factor_audits.what_the_record_shows: The June 16, 2023 incident involved Antioch Police Department officers per project_june16_2023_timeline.md. APD officers are peace officers under Penal Code § 830.1 (city police officers).
factor_audits.audit_status: PASSES — APD officers are peace officers under Penal Code § 830.1. This element is not the load-bearing one for the steward's case.

factor_audits.what_the_statute_requires: The peace officer must be IN UNIFORM at the time of giving the order.
factor_audits.what_the_record_shows: Per the case file, the responding APD officers on June 16, 2023 were in uniform.
factor_audits.audit_status: PASSES — uniform requirement satisfied. Not the load-bearing element.

factor_audits.factor_id: ELEMENT 6 — Performing duties pursuant to the Vehicle Code
factor_audits.what_the_statute_requires: The peace officer must be performing duties PURSUANT TO ANY OF THE PROVISIONS OF THIS CODE — meaning the Vehicle Code. An order issued in connection with some other type of investigation (e.g., a welfare check, a domestic disturbance, an arrest under the Penal Code) does NOT trigger § 2800(a) even if all other elements are satisfied. § 2800 lives in the Vehicle Code's Administration and Enforcement chapter and is structurally about traffic and vehicle inspection enforcement.
factor_audits.what_the_record_shows: The June 16, 2023 incident was, per the case file, NOT a traffic stop or vehicle inspection. It was a contact at a residence following a fabricated pretext. The officers were not performing Vehicle Code duties; they were responding to a non-Vehicle-Code call.
factor_audits.audit_question: Were the APD officers on June 16, 2023 performing Vehicle Code duties, or were they performing duties under some other code (most likely Penal Code or Welfare & Institutions Code)?
factor_audits.audit_status: CRITICAL — load-bearing audit item. If the officers were not performing Vehicle Code duties, § 2800(a) does not apply at all — regardless of any other element. § 2800 is the wrong statute for non-Vehicle-Code interactions. Any charge or consequence based on § 2800(a) would have to be re-characterized under whichever statute actually applied (e.g., Penal Code § 148 — resisting/delaying/obstructing a peace officer in the discharge of any duty).

steward_case_relevance_audit.audit_summary: TWO CRITICAL audit items: (1) ELEMENT 3 — was there any lawful basis for the officers' contact at all? (2) ELEMENT 6 — were the officers performing Vehicle Code duties, or were they performing duties under some other code? Both elements have to be satisfied for § 2800(a) to apply. If element 6 fails, § 2800 is the wrong statute regardless of any other consideration. If element 3 fails, the orders given during the contact were not lawful and § 2800 cannot have been violated. The case-file analysis of June 16, 2023 strongly suggests neither element 3 nor element 6 was satisfied, which would make any § 2800(a)-based consequence structurally defective. Steward review should specifically resolve both elements against the actual sequence of events that day.
